description: How Turnly cross-cuts between Japan and North Korea using stage directions and the sea.
content_html:
Two Countries, One Stage

Francis Turnly’s The Great Wave takes place across two countries and 24 years. To hold those two worlds simultaneously, Turnly relies on a single structural engine: cross-cutting. Scenes in Japan and North Korea alternate in quick succession, so the audience is never allowed to settle entirely into one world before the other pulls them back. This is not accidental restlessness — it is Turnly’s way of insisting that both lives are happening at the same time, that Hanako’s captivity and her family’s grief are not separate stories but a single wound.

Key Fact

Cross-cutting in The Great Wave creates parallel time: the audience watches Hanako adapting to life in North Korea at exactly the same moment that Reiko and Etsuko in Japan are refusing to accept she is dead. The two timelines are always in tension.

Stage Directions and the Sea

Turnly’s stage directions do far more than describe the set. They specify the sound of the sea as a recurring presence — waves are not decorative background noise but a reminder of the beach where Hanako disappeared. A director staging the play must decide how to realise this: a soundscape of waves can fade in and out to mark every transition between storylines, functioning as an audible signal that the two worlds are connected by that same sea. The stage direction does not merely set the scene — it instructs the entire company about the play’s emotional geography.

For a designer, realising the sea means a choice between approaches. A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey across the cyclorama can evoke the sea’s restlessness without requiring literal scenic waves. Some productions have used gobos to throw fragmented light patterns suggesting water moving across the floor — so even the North Korean compound scenes carry a visual trace of the sea the captive cannot reach.

Because the play spans 1979 to 2003, transitions between scenes must carry not just geographical shift (Japan to North Korea) but also temporal shift — sometimes several years pass in a single cut. Turnly’s stage directions use a combination of signals: a change in lighting state, a costume change visible to the audience, and a change in the physical bearing of the performers. A character who was upright and defiant in the preceding scene may enter the next one carrying the weight of another two years in their posture and pace.

For the director and designer this means agreeing a consistent vocabulary for transitions. If a blackout followed by a surge of wave sound means “time has passed,” that convention must be established early and held consistently — otherwise the audience loses its bearings across the play’s long arc. The blocking at the start of each new scene can itself signal time: a performer moving quickly to a new position suggests arrival in a new moment, while stillness as the lights rise signals that this scene begins mid-thought.

Code-Switching and Language as Subtext

One of Turnly’s most striking dramatic methods is the use of language as a marker of identity and coercion. In the North Korean scenes, English stands in for Japanese (the language Hanako speaks at home and later teaches) and stylised Korean signals that she is now living inside a system that wants to erase who she is. This code-switching is a form of subtext: every time Hanako speaks in the language she has been forced to learn, the audience feels the cost of her survival.

For a performer playing Hanako, the challenge is to carry the weight of that language shift in the body as well as the voice. A shift to Korean might be accompanied by a slight change in posture — a contained stillness, proxemics that keep her at a formal distance from the officials around her — so that the audience reads the language change as a kind of performance within performance, Hanako surviving by playing a role.

Key Fact

The play’s documentary realism roots — Turnly’s years of research with abductee families — shape the dramatic methods. The stage directions specify moments of bureaucratic procedure (interrogations, declarations, diplomatic meetings) with a precision that signals: this really happened to real people. That weight sits underneath every theatrical choice.

The Wave as Structural Metaphor

The play’s title is not set dressing. A wave is something that cannot be stopped once it begins; it moves people without asking permission; it appears to recede but leaves a changed landscape behind. Turnly uses this image structurally: the cross-cutting itself moves like a wave — rising in intensity as diplomatic events accelerate in the play’s second half, and finally cresting in the scenes around the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration. A director staging the play needs to feel and shape this rhythmic architecture, using the pace of scene transitions to build that wave towards its final breaking point.

Students sometimes describe cross-cutting as though it were simply a way to “keep the story moving.” Examiners reward much more than this. Cross-cutting in The Great Wave is a political act: by refusing to let the audience follow only Hanako’s story or only the family’s story, Turnly forces us to hold both in mind simultaneously — to feel the injustice of the gap between a family waiting for news and a daughter alive but unreachable. The technique creates dramatic irony and moral pressure on the audience, not just narrative variety.

When you discuss cross-cutting in an extended-response question, always explain its effect on the audience’s emotions and understanding, not just its technical description. Ask yourself: what does the audience know in this scene that the characters on stage do not? How does that knowledge create tension or grief?
exam_tip_html: For “Analyse the playwright’s intentions” questions (12 marks), the most common error is describing what happens in the play rather than analysing what Turnly wants the audience to think or feel at that moment. For cross-cutting and stage direction questions: never say “the playwright uses cross-cutting to show both storylines.” Instead say: “Turnly uses rapid cross-cutting to force the audience to hold both worlds simultaneously, creating a growing sense of moral outrage — the audience knows Hanako is alive while her family grieves, and that gap is the play’s central wound.” For extended staging responses (20 marks), always translate the playwright’s method into a specific design or performer choice: “I would use a wave-soundscape cross-fade as the transition cue, building in volume towards Act 2, so the audience physically feels the pressure of time passing.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cross-cutting between Japan and North Korea is Turnly’s central structural method: it forces the audience to experience both storylines simultaneously, creating dramatic irony and mounting moral pressure as the years pass.
  • Stage directions specify the sea — as sound, light and metaphor — as a recurring presence that connects the two worlds. Designers can realise this through a wave soundscape, a shifting blue-grey lighting wash, or gobo water-patterns that appear in both locations.
  • Code-switching between languages marks Hanako’s identity under coercion; a performer can carry this in their physicality and proxemics as well as their voice, making the language shift a visible as well as audible event.

practice_questions.text: Name the structural technique Turnly uses to move between scenes set in Japan and scenes set in North Korea.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: cross-cutting (accept: intercutting, parallel editing, alternating scenes).

practice_questions.text: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape uses layered sound to create atmosphere; 1 mark for explaining that it combines multiple audio elements (recorded, live, music, effects) simultaneously to suggest a place or emotional state.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Turnly uses stage directions about the sea to create meaning in The Great Wave. Refer to a specific moment or technique.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the sea as a recurring stage direction (1); explanation that it connects the two locations through a shared presence (1); analysis of what this means for the audience (creates dramatic irony — Hanako is near a sea she cannot cross back; 1); reference to how this could be realised in performance — soundscape, lighting, or design (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use the sound of the sea to mark transitions between scenes in The Great Wave. Refer to specific sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of wave sound as a transition cue (1); specific sound choice (e.g. volume swell, stereo positioning, recorded or live sound, reverb added for the North Korean scenes to signal distance; 1); effect on the audience (connects both storylines through a shared auditory image, building unease; 1); link to playwright’s intention (the sea as the site of loss and the barrier between worlds; 1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in using cross-cutting between the Japan scenes and the North Korea scenes throughout the play. What does he want the audience to understand and feel as a result of this structural choice?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response analyses multiple intentions simultaneously — the creation of dramatic irony (the audience knows Hanako is alive before the family does), the political argument that both lives are destroyed by the same state act, and the moral pressure on the audience generated by knowing more than the characters. Choices are anchored to named moments (e.g. the interrogation scenes cutting back to Reiko’s grief) and the analysis explains why Turnly wants that specific emotional effect. The response shows awareness of the play’s documentary roots: the cross-cutting insists that this is not fiction but a real, structural injustice.

Secure: identifies dramatic irony and the political argument; generally accurate about effect on audience; at least one named moment.

Developing: describes the cross-cutting technique and notes that it creates tension; limited analysis of intention; effect on audience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: lists what cross-cutting is without explaining what Turnly intends the audience to think or feel.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would stage the transitions between the Japan and North Korea scenes to communicate the passage of time and the ongoing separation of the family. Refer to set, lighting, sound and performer choices in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response proposes a coherent design vocabulary for transitions — e.g. a wave soundscape that swells and fades, a shifting blue-grey lighting state on the cyclorama, gobo water-patterns that persist in both locations, and performer choices (changed posture, pace, costume additions) that show ageing. Every choice is anchored to a named moment and explained in terms of its effect on the audience. The response shows directorial intention — the wave image is the controlling metaphor, realised consistently across all design disciplines. Structural awareness: the wave-rhythm builds towards the Pyongyang Declaration scenes.

Secure: at least three design disciplines addressed; generally concrete choices; at least one named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: relevant ideas about lighting and sound but choices are generic (“dark lighting,” “sad music”); few named moments; limited performer choices.

Emerging: describes the transitions in general terms without specific design or performer choices; no named moments; little directorial intention shown.

knowledge_checks.q: What does cross-cutting in The Great Wave force the audience to do?
options: Focus entirely on Hanako's story in North Korea
Hold both the Japan and North Korea storylines in mind at the same time
Follow the story in chronological order from 1979 to 2003
Concentrate on the historical context rather than the characters

knowledge_checks.q: In the North Korean scenes of The Great Wave, Hanako speaks in a language she has been forced to learn. What dramatic technique describes this shift between languages within the play?
Turnly's stage directions specify the sound of the _____ as a recurring presence that connects both locations in the play.
A _____ is a metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage, which a designer might use to suggest moving water.
Match each term to its definition:
right: Rapid alternation between two or more scenes in different places or times
Layered audio design that creates the atmosphere of a place
The physical and spatial relationship between performers on stage

flashcard_questions.q: What structural technique does Turnly use to keep the Japan and North Korea storylines running simultaneously?
flashcard_questions.a: Cross-cutting — rapidly alternating between the two locations.
Moving rapidly between scenes in different places or times, keeping both storylines present.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the sound of the sea represent in The Great Wave's stage directions?
flashcard_questions.a: The site of Hanako's disappearance and the barrier between her and her family.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
flashcard_questions.a: Layered audio — recorded, live, music, effects — that creates a sense of place or atmosphere.
A metal or glass plate in front of a lantern that projects a pattern of light onto the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What is code-switching in The Great Wave?
flashcard_questions.a: Hanako moving between Japanese and Korean, marking the pressure on her identity.

flashcard_questions.q: What years does The Great Wave's action span?

flashcard_questions.a: The physical and spatial relationship between performers, used to communicate status or emotion.
The complete picture of light on stage at one moment — its colour, direction, intensity and coverage.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the title The Great Wave significant for the play's structure?
flashcard_questions.a: A wave moves people without consent and leaves a changed landscape — mirroring the play's structure.
The planned pattern of performer movement and positioning on stage, created by the director.

flashcard_questions.q: What political event in 2002 drives the climax of The Great Wave?
flashcard_questions.a: The Pyongyang Declaration, when North Korea acknowledged the abductions.

glossary_terms.definition: A technique where a playwright cuts rapidly between two or more scenes in different times or places, keeping both storylines alive in the audience's mind at once.
A layered design of sound — recorded or live — that creates the atmosphere of a place or moment, using multiple audio elements simultaneously.
A broad wash of light covering the whole stage area, often used to create atmosphere or suggest an environment rather than illuminate specific actors.
A metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern or texture of light onto the stage surface.
Moving between two languages or registers within a scene, used in The Great Wave to signal identity, power, and the pressure to conform.
The physical and spatial relationship between two performers on stage, used to communicate status, emotional connection, or threat.
The complete picture of light on stage at a given moment — its colour, direction, intensity and coverage.
The pattern of movement and positioning of performers on stage, planned by the director to create meaning and guide the audience's eye.

items.description: NT behind-the-scenes on how the production team realised the sea as a continuous presence — directly relevant to how designers use projection and light for cross-cut transitions.

items.title: The Great Wave | Interview with Indhu Rubasingham and Francis Turnly
items.description: Turnly explains how the sea functions as a structural metaphor across the cross-cutting — the wave image as a rhythmic architecture that builds towards the Pyongyang Declaration.

items.title: An Introduction to Verbatim Theatre | National Theatre
items.description: NT introduction to verbatim and documentary theatre — useful context for understanding how Turnly's stage directions carry the weight of historical documentation.

items.title: Official Trailer: The Great Wave | National Theatre
items.description: Watch how the cross-cutting transitions are realised in the NT production — sea soundscape, lighting state changes, and blocking that communicates parallel time.

items.title: Grave of the Fireflies (1988)
items.description: Japanese animation about two children surviving wartime separation — emotionally parallel to the cross-cutting structure of The Great Wave's two worlds of endurance.

items.description: Use the spec's dramatic methods section to identify exactly which elements of cross-cutting and stage direction are assessed — and how to translate them into concrete staging answers.
